questions.q: A student draws a pie chart of dry air from the chapter's figures: nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, argon 0.93% and carbon dioxide 0.04%. She leaves the last slice, 'Others', blank. What figure should she write on it so that the whole pie is 100%?
questions.a: 100 - (78 + 21 + 0.93 + 0.04) = 0.03, which matches the 'Others 0.03%' slice of the chapter's Fig. 3.2. The slips are decimal-place errors (0.3 or 3) or an unrelated number (0.07).

questions.q: Astronomers study a rocky planet with no gases around it. Judging from what this chapter says the atmosphere does for the Earth, which pair of protections would that planet's surface lack?
questions.a: The chapter says the atmosphere shields us from harmful radiation including ultraviolet, and regulates temperature by trapping some of the Sun's energy. Gravity is what pulls the atmosphere down around the Earth; the atmosphere does not create it.
o: Shielding from the Sun's harmful radiation, and trapping part of its energy to regulate temperature
Pulling objects towards the ground by gravity, and keeping the planet turning at a steady speed day after day
Supplying water to the oceans of the planet, and fixing the planet's distance from the Sun for each year
Holding the planet's own gases down by gravity, and making the pull of its gravity stronger on the surface

questions.q: In a quiz, Tarun argues: 'Water vapour is only 0.1 to 0.4 per cent of the air, so it hardly matters.' Which reply is best supported by the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter gives 0.1 to 0.4 per cent as the usual range but says it varies, and says water vapour plays a significant role in cloud formation and precipitation. Small share does not mean small importance.
o: Its share is small, yet it plays a significant role in cloud formation and precipitation
Its share is small, so it matters only in places where nitrogen and oxygen are also scarce in the air
Its share is large in every place, so it matters far more than nitrogen and oxygen do in the air
Its share is fixed at 0.4 per cent everywhere, so rain depends on that one figure alone in every place

questions.q: A Class 9 student writes in her notebook: 'The atmosphere is the same at every height, so a climber at the top of a very high peak breathes air just like a person on the beach.' Which two statements from the chapter show her notebook entry is wrong?
questions.a: Page 40 states that the composition of the atmosphere also varies with altitude, and that the density of air is highest near the surface and decreases with altitude. The other options reverse or deny one of these.
o: Composition varies with altitude, and air is densest near the surface, thinning out with height
Composition is fixed at all heights, but air is thinnest near the surface and denser with height
Composition varies with altitude, but air has the same density from the surface right up to space
Composition is fixed at all heights, and air is densest at the very top of the atmosphere in space

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the composition of the atmosphere.
1. Nitrogen and oxygen are the two primary and most abundant gases in the atmosphere.
2. Carbon dioxide, at 0.04%, is the third most abundant gas, ahead of argon at 0.93%.
3. Besides gases, the atmosphere also contains water vapour and tiny dust particles.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false: 0.93% is more than 0.04%, so argon, not carbon dioxide, comes third. Statement 3 is true as the chapter states. Correct: 1 and 3 only.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
1, 2 and 3
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere.
Reason (R): The atmosphere is pulled down around the Earth by gravity.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true: the chapter's pie chart gives nitrogen 78%, and it says the atmosphere is pulled around the Earth by gravity. Gravity holds the whole blanket of air but does not explain why one gas has the largest share, so R is not the explanation.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: In the chapter's pie chart nitrogen is 78% and oxygen 21%, so these two gases together make up ___ per cent of the air.
Which of the following is NOT a role the chapter gives to the atmosphere?
questions.a: The chapter says the atmosphere is pulled down by gravity, a force that comes from the Earth's mass. The other three are roles stated on pages 39 and 40.
o: Producing the force that pulls the atmosphere down around the Earth
Shielding living beings from ultraviolet radiation from the Sun
Supporting cloud formation and precipitation through water vapour
Regulating the Earth's temperature by trapping some of the Sun's energy

questions.q: True or False: The share of water vapour in the atmosphere is fixed, at 0.1 to 0.4 per cent, everywhere on the Earth. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the amount of water vapour varies; 0.1 to 0.4 per cent is only the range in which it generally lies.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the amount varies from place to place and time to time; the range is only what it generally is

questions.q: (a) Add the shares of nitrogen (78%), oxygen (21%), argon (0.93%) and carbon dioxide (0.04%) shown in the chapter's pie chart. (b) Name two of the gases that must share what is left.
questions.a: (a) 78 + 21 + 0.93 + 0.04 = 99.97 per cent. (b) What is left is 0.03 per cent, shared by the 'others' such as helium, neon, krypton, xenon, ozone and hydrogen; any two.
s: Sum 99.97 per cent, leaving 0.03
Any two of helium, neon, krypton, xenon, ozone, hydrogen

questions.q: (a) Which force keeps the atmosphere around the Earth? (b) The density of air is highest near the surface. Say how density changes as you go up and what that tells you about where most of the air is found.
questions.a: (a) Gravity. (b) Density decreases with altitude, so most of the air lies close to the Earth's surface.
s: Gravity
Density falls with height, so most air is near the surface

questions.q: The atmosphere protects us in two different ways, one against the Sun's radiation and one against loss of heat. State each protection in one line.
questions.a: It shields us from harmful radiation, including ultraviolet radiation, coming from the Sun. It regulates the Earth's temperature by trapping some of the Sun's energy and preventing it from escaping back into space.
s: Shields from harmful radiation including ultraviolet
Traps some of the Sun's energy and stops it escaping into space

questions.q: The chapter's 'Think About It' asks what would happen if there were no atmosphere. Give two different consequences that follow from the chapter's own statements.
questions.a: Any two of: no shield against harmful radiation including ultraviolet; the Earth's energy would not be trapped, so temperature would not be regulated; no water vapour, so no clouds and no precipitation; no mixture of gases for living beings to survive.
s: First consequence tied to a stated role
Second, different consequence tied to a stated role

questions.q: Meena says, 'Oxygen is the most abundant gas in the air because every living being needs it to survive.' Test her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: No, the claim is wrong. Oxygen is 21 per cent, while nitrogen is 78 per cent, so nitrogen is the most abundant. Need for a gas does not decide its share; the chapter calls nitrogen and oxygen the two most abundant gases, with nitrogen larger.
s: Verdict: No
Figures: oxygen 21%, nitrogen 78%
Need does not decide abundance

questions.q: Give three reasons, each taken from the chapter, why the atmosphere is called vital for the survival of living beings.
questions.a: It is a mixture of gases (nitrogen, oxygen and others) that living beings need; it shields us from harmful radiation including ultraviolet; it regulates temperature by trapping the Sun's energy. (Water vapour for clouds and rain is also acceptable.)
s: A mixture of gases needed for life
Shield against harmful radiation
Regulates temperature by trapping energy

questions.q: On a humid evening a weather station records 0.4 per cent water vapour in the air; the next dry morning it records 0.1 per cent. (i) Is this consistent with the chapter? (ii) Name two processes in which water vapour plays a significant part.
questions.a: (i) Yes: the chapter says water vapour varies and generally ranges from 0.1 to 0.4 per cent, so both readings lie in the range. (ii) Cloud formation and precipitation.
s: Consistent: it varies within 0.1 to 0.4 per cent
Cloud formation
Precipitation

questions.q: Justify the statement: 'The atmosphere is both a protector and a supplier for living beings.' Use the chapter.
questions.a: Blanket of air held by gravity around the Earth; it protects by shielding from ultraviolet and other harmful radiation; it protects by trapping some of the Sun's energy to regulate temperature; it supplies the gases (mainly nitrogen and oxygen) essential for life; it supplies water vapour for clouds and precipitation.
s: Atmosphere is a blanket of air held around the Earth by gravity
Protector: shields from harmful radiation including ultraviolet
Protector: traps Sun's energy and regulates temperature
Supplier: nitrogen and oxygen essential to life
Supplier: water vapour for clouds and precipitation

questions.q: A teacher builds a class model of the air with 10,000 beads, using the chapter's pie-chart percentages: nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, argon 0.93%, carbon dioxide 0.04%, others 0.03%. (i) Work out how many beads of each kind are needed. (ii) Show that the total is 10,000. (iii) Explain why the carbon dioxide and 'others' slices of the pie chart are hard to see, and what a student looking at the model would notice about them.
questions.a: (i) Nitrogen 7800, oxygen 2100, argon 93, carbon dioxide 4, others 3. (ii) 7800 + 2100 + 93 + 4 + 3 = 10,000. (iii) Their shares are tiny (0.04% and 0.03%), so the slices are thin lines; in the model there would be only 4 and 3 beads among 10,000, while nitrogen and oxygen fill almost all of the model.
s: Nitrogen 7800 and oxygen 2100 beads
Argon 93, carbon dioxide 4, others 3 beads
Total shown to be 10,000
Reason the slices are thin: shares 0.04% and 0.03%
Observation: 4 and 3 beads among 10,000, nitrogen and oxygen dominate

questions.q:
A school's science club prepared three corridor posters on the atmosphere. Poster 1 says, 'Nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, the rest less than 1%.' Poster 2 says, 'The air shields us from ultraviolet radiation and keeps the Earth's temperature steady.' Poster 3 says, 'Water vapour makes clouds and rain, and it is always exactly 0.4 per cent.' The club has wall space for only two posters.
(a) By how many times is nitrogen larger than oxygen on Poster 1? Give the answer to one decimal place.
(b) Which poster contains an error, and what is it?
(c) Which role of the atmosphere is shown on Poster 2 but missing from the other two?
(d) Decide which two posters should go up, and justify your choice, saying what the unchosen poster would have taught.
questions.a: (a) 78 / 21 is about 3.7 times. (b) Poster 3: water vapour is not fixed; it varies, generally from 0.1 to 0.4 per cent. (c) Protection: shielding from harmful radiation (and temperature regulation). (d) Either defensible, e.g. Posters 1 and 2 (composition plus protection) if the correction of Poster 3 is not possible, or Posters 2 and 3 corrected; credit a judgement that uses (a) to (c) and names what the left-out poster would teach (composition figures, protection, or the role of water vapour in rain).
s: About 3.7 times (78/21)
Poster 3: water vapour varies, 0.1 to 0.4 per cent is only a general range
Poster 2: shield from harmful radiation / temperature regulation
Justified choice of two posters with what the third would teach

questions.q:
The chapter asks, 'Can you imagine what would happen if there were no atmosphere?' Four students in a Class 9 discussion answer. Anjali: 'There would be no clouds or rain.' Bilal: 'Nothing would stop the Sun's harmful radiation reaching us.' Chetan: 'The Earth would lose the gravity that pulls things to the ground.' Divya: 'The Sun's energy would no longer be trapped, so the temperature would not be regulated.' The teacher can discuss only two answers in the remaining time.
(a) Which student's answer is not supported by the chapter, and why?
(b) Name the part of the air that Anjali's answer depends on.
(c) Which two answers are about the atmosphere as a protector of life?
(d) Choose the two answers the teacher should discuss for a class living in a dry region, and justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) Chetan: gravity is the Earth's own force that pulls the atmosphere down; the atmosphere does not produce it. (b) Water vapour, which plays a significant role in cloud formation and precipitation. (c) Bilal (shield from radiation) and Divya (trapping energy / temperature regulation). (d) Either choice is defensible: for a dry region, Anjali's (rain depends on water vapour) plus one protector answer is reasonable; or the two protector answers if the class wants to see the roles that apply everywhere. The answer must use the chapter and give a reason for leaving the others.
s: Chetan: gravity pulls the atmosphere, the atmosphere does not create it
Water vapour (cloud formation and precipitation)
Bilal and Divya
Justified selection of two answers with a reason

questions.q: A model-maker draws the atmosphere with 1 cm standing for 10 km. Using the heights in the chapter (the troposphere ends at about 12 km and the stratosphere extends up to 50 km), how thick should she draw the stratosphere strip?
questions.a: The stratosphere runs from about 12 km to 50 km, so it is 38 km thick, which is 3.8 cm at 1 cm per 10 km. 5.0 cm is the height of its top edge, 1.2 cm the troposphere's height, and 3.0 cm the thickness of the mesosphere.
o: 3.8 cm
5.0 cm
1.2 cm
3.0 cm

questions.q: Aarti records the temperature on a chart as a probe climbs from the ground to 100 km, and notes where it falls with height. According to the chapter, in which layers will she find the temperature falling as height increases?
questions.a: The 'Don't miss out' box on page 42 says temperature decreases with altitude only in the troposphere and mesosphere. The thermosphere is the layer in which it rises very rapidly, but it is not the only layer in which it fails to fall.
o: Only in the troposphere and the mesosphere
In the troposphere, the stratosphere and the mesosphere alike
Only in the stratosphere and the thermosphere together
In every layer except the thermosphere, where it rises

questions.q: A radio amateur in Pune notices that her signal, sent upwards, returns towards the ground far away. Which layer of the atmosphere does the chapter credit with this help to radio transmission?
questions.a: Page 42 says the thermosphere helps radio transmission by reflecting radio waves back towards the Earth, and that the ionosphere is a part of it. The other layers are given other features (ozone, weather, very thin air).
o: The thermosphere, which reflects radio waves back towards the Earth
The stratosphere, because its ozone returns the radio waves to the ground
The troposphere, because its clouds and water vapour bounce the signal back
The exosphere, because its very thin air turns the radio waves back around

questions.q: A pilot-training manual says: 'Cruise in the layer where there are no clouds and no weather disturbances.' A trainee chooses the layer where rain, fog and hail occur because 'nearly all the air is there'. What is the best correction using the chapter?
questions.a: Rainfall, fog and hail occur in the troposphere. The stratosphere above it is free of clouds and weather disturbances and is described as ideal for flying aeroplanes.
o: That layer, the troposphere, has the weather; the cloud-free layer above it, the stratosphere, suits aeroplanes
That layer, the stratosphere, has the weather; the cloud-free layer below it, the troposphere, suits aeroplanes
That layer, the troposphere, is cloud-free; the weather is found in the mesosphere above it, where aeroplanes fly
That layer, the mesosphere, has the weather; the cloud-free layer below it, the stratosphere, suits aeroplanes

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the layers of the atmosphere.
1. Aeroplanes fly in the troposphere because it is the layer free of clouds and weather disturbances.
2. The exosphere is the uppermost layer, with very thin air from which light gases like helium and hydrogen float into space.
3. In the thermosphere the temperature decreases as height increases.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: the cloud-free layer ideal for aeroplanes is the stratosphere. Statement 2 is true. Statement 3 is false: in the thermosphere the temperature rises very rapidly with height. Correct: 2 only.
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the thermosphere the temperature rises very rapidly with increasing altitude.
Reason (R): The gas molecules in the thermosphere absorb the X-rays and short-wave ultraviolet radiation of the Sun.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A. The chapter gives the absorption of X-rays and short-wave ultraviolet radiation as the reason for the rapid rise in temperature in this layer.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: The stratosphere extends up to 50 km and the troposphere has an average height of about 12 km, so the stratosphere is about ___ km thick.

Match each layer in Column I with the feature in Column II.
1. Troposphere
2. Stratosphere
3. Mesosphere
4. Thermosphere
a. Contains the ozone layer that filters ultraviolet radiation
b. Reflects radio waves towards the Earth
c. Burns up most meteorites entering from space
d. Holds most of the water vapour and clouds
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: Troposphere: most water vapour and clouds; stratosphere: ozone layer; mesosphere: most meteorites burn up; thermosphere: reflects radio waves.

questions.q: True or False: The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere, and this is the reason why the stratosphere filters out some of the Sun's harmful radiation. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the stratosphere contains a layer of ozone gas, which shields us by filtering the Sun's harmful radiation, including ultraviolet radiation.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: ozone gas in the stratosphere filters the harmful radiation, including ultraviolet

questions.q: (a) Using the chapter's heights (troposphere up to about 12 km, stratosphere up to 50 km, mesosphere up to 80 km), find the thickness of the stratosphere and of the mesosphere. (b) Which of the two is thicker, and by how many kilometres?
questions.a: (a) Stratosphere 50 - 12 = 38 km; mesosphere 80 - 50 = 30 km. (b) The stratosphere is thicker, by 8 km.
s: Stratosphere 38 km and mesosphere 30 km
Stratosphere thicker, by 8 km

questions.q: (a) In which layer do aeroplanes fly? (b) Give the chapter's reason, and say what is found in the layer just below it that makes it less suitable.
questions.a: (a) The stratosphere. (b) It is free of clouds and other weather disturbances; the troposphere below has the clouds and weather phenomena such as rainfall, fog and hail.
s: Stratosphere
Free of clouds and disturbances, unlike the troposphere with rain, fog and hail

questions.q: The troposphere and the mesosphere are alike in one way and different in another. State the likeness and one difference.
questions.a: Alike: in both, temperature decreases with increasing altitude. Different: the troposphere (average height about 12 km) has the air we breathe, most water vapour and clouds and nearly all weather, while the mesosphere (up to 80 km) is where most meteorites burn up.
s: Likeness: temperature falls with altitude in both
A valid difference (weather / air we breathe versus meteorites burning)

questions.q: Why are coloured lights called auroras seen near the poles and not all over the Earth? Answer in two steps and name the layer where they occur.
questions.a: The solar wind (charged particles from the Sun) reaching the Earth's atmosphere is directed towards the magnetic poles; there the particles interact with atmospheric gases and each gas glows with a particular colour. This happens in the thermosphere.
s: Solar wind is directed towards the magnetic poles
Particles interact with gases that glow in colours; thermosphere

questions.q: Write three clues, each taken from the chapter, that would let a classmate identify the thermosphere without your using its name.
questions.a: Any three of: it extends from 80 to 700 km; temperature rises very rapidly with height; its gas molecules absorb X-rays and short-wave ultraviolet radiation; it reflects radio waves back to the Earth; it contains the ionosphere; auroras occur in it.
s: First valid clue
Second valid clue
Third valid clue

questions.q: Imran says, 'The layers of the atmosphere are marked out by changes in temperature and density with height, and temperature falls with height in only two of the five.' Is he right? Support your answer with the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says the layers are defined on the basis of changes in temperature and density with increasing altitude, and the 'Don't miss out' box says temperature decreases with altitude only in the troposphere and the mesosphere, which are two of the five.
s: Verdict: Yes
Layers defined by temperature and density changes
Temperature falls only in troposphere and mesosphere

questions.q: A report says that rain was observed falling from clouds at a height of 30 km. Show that the report cannot be right according to the chapter.
questions.a: At 30 km the layer is the stratosphere (it extends up to 50 km, above the troposphere that ends at about 12 km). The stratosphere is free of clouds and other weather disturbances, while rainfall, fog and hail occur in the troposphere. So rain from clouds at 30 km is not possible.
s: 30 km lies in the stratosphere (above about 12 km, below 50 km)
The stratosphere is free of clouds and weather disturbances
Rainfall occurs in the troposphere, so the report fails

questions.q: Compare the troposphere and the stratosphere on height, temperature change with height, what each contains and what each is useful for, and explain why the difference matters to people.
questions.a: Height: troposphere about 12 km on average; stratosphere extends from there up to 50 km. Temperature: in the troposphere it decreases with altitude; the stratosphere is not one of the two layers in which temperature decreases. Contents: the troposphere has the air we breathe, most water vapour and clouds and nearly all weather phenomena; the stratosphere has the ozone layer and no clouds. Use: weather and breathing happen in the troposphere; aeroplanes fly in the stratosphere and ozone filters ultraviolet. It matters because life and weather depend on the lower layer while the upper one protects and gives safe flying.
s: Heights of the two layers
Temperature behaviour with height
What each contains (weather and breathable air; ozone and no clouds)
Use of each (weather and life; aeroplanes and UV filtering)
Why the difference matters to people

questions.q: Describe the five layers of the atmosphere from the ground upwards. For each layer give its upper limit (where the chapter gives one) and one feature. Then say which layers are separated by a transition zone named in the chapter.
questions.a: Troposphere: about 12 km; weather, air we breathe. Stratosphere: up to 50 km; ozone layer, no clouds. Mesosphere: up to 80 km; meteorites burn up, temperature falls. Thermosphere: 80 to 700 km; temperature rises rapidly, reflects radio waves, auroras. Exosphere: uppermost, very thin air, helium and hydrogen float away. The tropopause separates the troposphere from the stratosphere, and the stratopause separates the stratosphere from the mesosphere.
s: Troposphere with limit and a feature
Stratosphere with limit and a feature
Mesosphere with limit and a feature
Thermosphere and exosphere with a feature each
Tropopause (tropo/strato) and stratopause (strato/meso)

questions.q:
A flying club plans four unmanned test flights, each going straight up: Flight 1 to 8 km, Flight 2 to 30 km, Flight 3 to 65 km and Flight 4 to 200 km. The club has two aims. Aim X is a smooth cruise with no clouds or weather disturbances. Aim Y is a control link in which a radio signal is reflected back to the ground. Money is enough for one flight only.
(a) Name the layer in which each flight ends.
(b) Which flight can meet Aim X, and which feature of its layer explains this?
(c) Which flight can meet Aim Y, and which feature of its layer explains this?
(d) Decide which one flight the club should fund, and justify the choice by saying what the club gives up.
questions.a: (a) Flight 1: troposphere; Flight 2: stratosphere; Flight 3: mesosphere; Flight 4: thermosphere. (b) Flight 2: the stratosphere is free of clouds and weather disturbances. (c) Flight 4: the thermosphere reflects radio waves back towards the Earth. (d) Either is defensible: funding Flight 2 secures the smooth cruise but loses the reflected radio link; funding Flight 4 secures the link but loses the cloud-free cruise. Credit a decision that names this trade-off.
s: Four layers named correctly
Flight 2 and the cloud-free stratosphere
Flight 4 and radio-wave reflection in the thermosphere
Decision that names what is given up

questions.q:
A museum wants a wall display of the atmosphere to scale, up to the top of the thermosphere (700 km). The wall is 3 m (300 cm) tall. Two scales are being compared. Scale X: 1 cm stands for 1 km. Scale Y: 1 cm stands for 5 km. The troposphere is taken as 12 km thick and the thermosphere as extending from 80 km to 700 km.
(a) On Scale X, how tall would the top of the thermosphere be, and would it fit on the wall?
(b) On Scale Y, how thick would the troposphere strip be?
(c) On Scale Y, how thick would the thermosphere strip be?
(d) Decide which scale the museum should use, and justify your choice using both layers.
questions.a: (a) 700 cm = 7 m, which is more than the 3 m wall, so it does not fit. (b) 12 / 5 = 2.4 cm. (c) (700 - 80) / 5 = 124 cm. (d) Scale Y fits the whole display (140 cm to the top of the thermosphere) but the troposphere, where weather occurs, is only a thin 2.4 cm strip; Scale X shows the troposphere as 12 cm but cannot show the thermosphere. Credit either choice that uses these figures and names the loss, or a compromise such as a separate enlarged inset for the troposphere.
s: 7 m, does not fit on the wall
2.4 cm
124 cm
Decision justified with both strips and what is lost

questions.q: A farmer on a hilltop measures the wind at 45 km/h. Large branches sway and his umbrella is hard to hold. Using the chapter's Table 3.1, which category does this wind belong to?
questions.a: 45 km/h lies between 39 and 49 km/h, the strong breeze, whose effects are large branches swaying and umbrellas difficult to use. A light breeze only rustles leaves, a storm causes widespread damage, and calm lets smoke rise vertically.
o: Strong breeze, 39 to 49 km/h
Light breeze, 6 to 11 km/h, so leaves rustle
Storm, 103 to 117 km/h, so damage is widespread
Calm, 0 to 1 km/h, so smoke rises straight up

questions.q: At 3 p.m. on a summer day in a coastal town, fishermen feel a cool wind blowing from the water towards the shore. Which explanation fits the chapter?
questions.a: A sea breeze blows from sea to land during the day, especially in the afternoon, when the land is relatively warmer than the sea. That makes a low-pressure region over the land, and air moves from high to low pressure.
o: The land has become warmer than the sea, so a low-pressure region forms over the land and the wind blows in from the sea
The land has become cooler than the sea, so a high-pressure region forms over the land and the wind blows in from the sea
The sea has become warmer than the land, so a low-pressure region forms over the sea and the wind blows in from the land
The land has become warmer than the sea, so a high-pressure region forms over the land and the wind blows out to the sea

questions.q: A news bulletin makes four remarks about Nagpur. Which one is a statement about its climate and not about its weather?
questions.a: Climate is the sum total of weather conditions and variations over a large area for an extended period, usually thirty years or more. The other remarks describe hour-to-hour or day-to-day conditions, which is weather.
o: Over the last thirty years Nagpur has averaged about 124 cm of rain a year
This afternoon the sky was bright and then it drizzled for ten minutes
The temperature touched 35 degrees Celsius at noon and cooled after the rain
Tomorrow morning is expected to be windy with a few passing clouds

questions.q: Over Place P the air has been heated, has risen and spread out. Over Place Q the air is cold, heavy and sinking. According to the chapter, what should a forecaster expect?
questions.a: Where air heats and rises there is low pressure, associated with cloudy skies and wet weather; where cold air sinks there is high pressure, associated with clear and sunny skies. Air always moves from high pressure to low pressure, so from Q to P.
o: Cloudy, wet weather at P, clear sunny skies at Q, and air moving from Q towards P
Clear sunny skies at P, cloudy wet weather at Q, and air moving from P towards Q
Cloudy, wet weather at P, clear sunny skies at Q, and air moving from P towards Q
Clear sunny skies at both places, with air moving from Q towards P

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the elements of weather and climate.
1. Rain is the least common form of precipitation, ahead only of hail.
2. A wind that blows from the west is called a westerly, because winds are named after the direction they blow from.
3. A sea breeze blows from the sea to the land during the day, when the land is relatively warmer than the sea.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: rain is the most common form of precipitation. Statements 2 and 3 are as the chapter states. Correct: 2 and 3 only.
o: 2 and 3 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3
2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A high-pressure area is usually associated with clear and sunny skies.
Reason (R): In a high-pressure area the air is warm and light, so it rises and forms clouds.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true: cold, heavy air sinks to create a high-pressure area with clear and sunny skies. R is false: it describes a low-pressure area, where heated air rises, and so it is the reverse of what happens in a high-pressure area.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A wind blowing from the east towards the west is named after the direction it comes from, so it is called an ___ wind.
questions.a: easterly

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five major elements of the atmosphere that the chapter names as impacting human life on the Earth?
questions.a: The five elements named are temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind and atmospheric pressure. Insolation, the incoming solar energy intercepted by the Earth, is a factor affecting the distribution of temperature, not one of the five elements.
o: Insolation
Humidity
Atmospheric pressure
Precipitation

questions.q: True or False: A land breeze blows from the sea to the land at night, because the land cools faster than the sea. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: False. The reason given is correct, but the direction is the other way: a land breeze blows from land to sea during the night, because the land cools faster than the sea.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: it blows from land to sea at night

questions.q: On a weather map, the pressure at Town P is 996 and at Town Q is 1008 (in the units of the chapter's Fig. 3.7). (a) In which direction will the wind blow? (b) What kind of weather is associated with the lower pressure?
questions.a: (a) From Q to P, because air moves from a high-pressure area to a low-pressure area. (b) Low pressure is associated with cloudy skies and wet weather.
s: Wind from Q (high) to P (low)
Cloudy skies and wet weather at the low-pressure place

questions.q: (a) At 1 km/h, in which category of Table 3.1 does the wind fall, and what do you see? (b) If the wind rises to 40 km/h, name the new category and give one effect.
questions.a: (a) Calm: smoke rises vertically. (b) Strong breeze: large branches sway in the wind / umbrellas are difficult to use.
s: Calm, smoke rises vertically
Strong breeze with one effect

questions.q: The air above us exerts a significant force on our bodies, yet we do not feel it. Give the chapter's explanation.
questions.a: Air presses on us from all sides, and our bodies exert a counter-pressure in response; the pressure inside our bodies is equal to the atmospheric pressure and cancels the pressure from outside.
s: Air presses from all sides
The pressure inside the body equals and cancels the outside pressure

questions.q: Distinguish between weather and climate, giving a time span for each.
questions.a: Weather is the hour-to-hour and day-to-day condition of the atmosphere. Climate is the sum total of weather conditions and variations over a large area for an extended period, usually thirty years or more.
s: Weather: hour-to-hour and day-to-day conditions
Climate: long-term sum total over a large area, usually thirty years or more

questions.q: Farida says, 'Precipitation means only rain, and rain always lowers the temperature of a place.' How far is she right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. Rain does lower the temperature of a place, as the chapter says. But precipitation is not only rain: it includes drizzle, rain, snow, sleet and hail; rain is only the most common form.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right: rain lowers temperature
Wrong: precipitation also includes drizzle, snow, sleet, hail

questions.q: A weather report ends with: 'Pressure is low, the sky is cloudy and rain is likely.' Describe a situation that would produce these conditions, covering the temperature of the air, its movement and where the winds come from.
questions.a: The air over the place has been heated; it rises, which creates a low-pressure area, associated with cloudy skies and wet weather. Winds then blow into it from surrounding higher-pressure areas, because air moves from high to low pressure.
s: Air heated and rising, creating low pressure
Low pressure linked with cloud and wet weather
Wind moves in from higher-pressure surroundings

questions.q: A student writes, 'At midnight the sea breeze keeps the town cool.' Show that this cannot be right, using the chapter.
questions.a: A sea breeze blows from sea to land during the day, especially in the afternoon, when the land is relatively warmer than the sea, giving low pressure over land. At night the land cools faster than the sea, so the wind blows from land to sea; that is a land breeze. A sea breeze at midnight does not occur.
s: Sea breeze belongs to the day, when the land is warmer
At night land cools faster, the situation reverses
The night wind is the land breeze, so the sentence is wrong

questions.q: On a humid day clothes take longer to dry and sweat evaporates more slowly. Explain this with the chapter's idea of humidity and say how the warmth of the air is linked to it.
questions.a: Humidity is the presence of water vapour in the air, creating moisture; when the levels of water vapour are high the air is humid, so clothes and sweat lose water more slowly. The chapter adds that warmer air can hold more water vapour, so its humidity can be higher.
s: Humidity means water vapour in the air
High vapour slows drying of clothes and evaporation of sweat
Warmer air can hold more water vapour

questions.q: Explain how differences in air pressure produce wind and how this gives the sea breeze by day and the land breeze at night. State what these local winds do for the climate of the coast.
questions.a: Hot air rises, creating low pressure; cold air is heavy and sinks, creating high pressure. Wind is air moving from high to low pressure. By day the land is warmer than the sea, low pressure forms over land, and the sea breeze blows from sea to land. At night the land cools faster, and the land breeze blows from land to sea at low speed because the temperature and pressure difference is small. These local winds create moderate climatic conditions in the coastal region.
s: Heated air rises (low pressure), cold air sinks (high pressure)
Wind is movement from high to low pressure
Sea breeze by day, with the land warmer
Land breeze at night, land cools faster, low speed
Local winds give moderate climate to the coast

questions.q: A school weather club recorded the yearly rainfall of its town for five years: 120 cm, 96 cm, 143 cm, 88 cm and 110 cm. (i) Find the average. (ii) A member says this average is the town's climate. Using the chapter, explain whether five years is enough, and how many more years of records would reach the usual period. (iii) Say what the 143 cm year is, in the chapter's terms, and what the club should do before saying that the climate has changed.
questions.a: (i) (120 + 96 + 143 + 88 + 110) / 5 = 557 / 5 = 111.4 cm. (ii) Climate is the sum total of weather conditions over an extended period, usually thirty years or more, so five years is too short; 25 more years are needed to reach thirty. (iii) The 143 cm year is one year's variation in the weather record, not the climate by itself; the club should keep recording and judge by the long-term record before claiming a change.
s: Average 111.4 cm
Five years too short; climate usually thirty years or more
25 more years needed
143 cm is a variation of one year, not the climate
Keep recording and judge the long-term record

questions.q:
A fishing cooperative in a coastal town studies its wind log (units as in the chapter's Fig. 3.7). At 3 p.m. the pressure over the land is 1004 and over the sea 1008. At 3 a.m. the pressure over the land is 1008 and over the sea 1006. Boats can go out at night and return in the afternoon, or the cooperative can fit engines.
(a) At 3 p.m., from where to where does the wind blow, and what is it called?
(b) At 3 a.m., from where to where does the wind blow, and what is it called?
(c) At which hour is the pressure difference smaller, and what does the chapter say about the speed of that wind?
(d) The cooperative can afford to fit engines on only half of its boats. Decide whether engines should go on boats that sail out at night or on boats that return in the afternoon, and justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) From sea (1008) to land (1004): the sea breeze. (b) From land (1008) to sea (1006): the land breeze. (c) At 3 a.m. the difference is 2 against 4 at 3 p.m.; the chapter says the land breeze has a low speed because the difference in temperature and pressure is low. (d) Either choice is defensible if it uses (a) to (c): engines on the night boats because the outgoing land breeze is gentle and the boats may be slow to leave; or on the returning boats because the sea breeze is a day wind that blows only in the right direction while the land is warmer. Credit the use of both winds' direction and speed.
s: 3 p.m.: sea to land, sea breeze
3 a.m.: land to sea, land breeze
Difference 2 at 3 a.m. against 4; land breeze has low speed
Reasoned choice of boats for engines using direction and speed

questions.q:
A school plans a January sports meet and compares three stations from the chapter's representative data. Leh (34 degrees N, altitude 3506 m): January temperature -8.5 degrees Celsius, January rainfall 1.0 cm. Delhi (29 degrees N): 14.4 degrees Celsius, 2.5 cm. Chennai (13 degrees N): 24.5 degrees Celsius, 4.6 cm.
(a) How much warmer is Chennai than Leh in January?
(b) Does the order of January temperature follow the order of distance from the equator, and which idea from the chapter explains this?
(c) Leh is also very high above sea level; what does the chapter say about temperature and altitude in the layer where weather occurs?
(d) The school can book only one of Delhi and Chennai for its meet. Decide which, using both the temperature and the rainfall figures, and say what the other place offers.
questions.a: (a) 24.5 - (-8.5) = 33.0 degrees Celsius. (b) Yes: temperature falls from Chennai to Delhi to Leh as one moves away from the equator, because insolation decreases from the equator towards the poles. (c) In the troposphere temperature decreases with increasing altitude, so Leh's height adds to its cold. (d) Either is defensible: Delhi is cooler (14.4) and drier (2.5 cm) in January, Chennai is warmer (24.5) but wetter (4.6 cm). Credit a decision that weighs both figures and names what the other place offers.
s: 33.0 degrees Celsius
Yes; insolation decreases from equator to poles
Temperature decreases with altitude in the troposphere
Decision weighing temperature and rainfall, naming what the other offers

questions.q: A family travels in north-western India in late October and again in November, and finds the days cloudless both times. Which IMD season are they in, and what is it also called?
questions.a: The post-monsoon season lasts from October to December, and the chapter says that in north-western India October and November are usually cloudless. It is also called the retreating monsoon; the advancing monsoon is the June to September season.
o: Post-monsoon, also called the retreating monsoon
Monsoon, also called the advancing monsoon of the rainy months
Winter, also called the pre-monsoon season before the rains
Summer, also called the retreating monsoon of the dry months

questions.q: Two cousins compare notes. Reena lives in a western region and Tarun in a northern region. Each says, 'The hottest month in my region comes just before the rains.' According to the chapter, which pair of hottest months is correct?
questions.a: The chapter says that in western and southern regions the hottest month is April, while in northern regions it is May. Treating one month as hottest for the whole country, or swapping the two, are the slips.
o: April for Reena's western region and May for Tarun's northern region
May for Reena's western region and April for Tarun's northern region
April for both regions, because the pre-monsoon season starts in that month
May for both regions, because the pre-monsoon season ends in that month

questions.q: A temple committee in a village celebrates a festival in the month of Mārgaśhīrṣha of the Indian calendar. Using the chapter's Table 3.2, which traditional season and which Gregorian months does this fall in?
questions.a: Table 3.2 pairs Mārgaśhīrṣha and Pauṣha with the season Hemanta, in November and December. The other options are the seasons of the neighbouring months in the table.
o: Hemanta, which falls in November and December
Śharad, which falls in September and October
Śhiśhira, which falls in January and February
Varṣhā, which falls in July and August

questions.q: A school in a Himalayan state shows five or six seasons on its calendar, while a school in the plains shows four. A student says the hill school's calendar is a mistake. What does the chapter say that settles this?
questions.a: The chapter says the Himalayan states, being more temperate, experience two additional seasons, autumn and spring, beyond the four IMD seasons.
o: The Himalayan states are more temperate and have two more seasons, autumn and spring
The Himalayan states are hotter and so lose the winter season, while keeping spring and autumn
The Himalayan states lie outside the monsoon region and so follow only the traditional calendar
The Himalayan states are higher and so have a longer monsoon, which is split into two seasons

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the seasons of India.
1. The summer or pre-monsoon season spans from April to June, or up to July in north-western India.
2. The post-monsoon season is also described as the retreating monsoon.
3. The Himalayan states, being more temperate, experience autumn and spring as two additional seasons.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are given in the chapter: the summer season runs April to June or up to July in the north-west; post-monsoon is labelled 'Retreating monsoon'; the Himalayan states have autumn and spring as well. Correct: all three.
o: 1, 2 and 3
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In every part of India the hottest month of the year is May.
Reason (R): In northern regions the hottest month is May.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: in western and southern regions the hottest month is April. R is true: the chapter says that in northern regions it is May. A true reason does not make the sweeping assertion true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: The traditional season that comes right after Varṣhā (July and August) in the chapter's table is ___.
questions.a: Sharad

questions.q:
Match each IMD season in Column I with the description in Column II.
1. Winter
2. Summer or pre-monsoon
3. Monsoon or rainy
4. Post-monsoon
a. The humid south-west monsoon sweeps across the country, June to September
b. In western and southern regions its hottest month is April
c. In north-western India October and November are usually cloudless
d. Lasts from December to early April, coldest in December and January
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: Winter: December to early April, coldest in December and January. Summer: April to June, hottest month April in the west and south. Monsoon: June to September. Post-monsoon: October to December, cloudless in the north-west in October and November.

questions.q: True or False: The traditional six Indian seasons are based on dividing the 12 months of the year into six parts, so each is about two months long. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the traditional seasons are based on the astronomical division of the 12 months into six parts, each about two months long; 6 x 2 = 12.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: 12 months divided into six parts gives about two months each

questions.q: (a) Name the traditional season of the Gregorian months May and June. (b) Which IMD season do those same two months fall in, and what is the IMD's hottest month for northern regions?
questions.a: (a) Grīṣhma (Jyeṣhṭha-Āṣhāḍha). (b) The summer or pre-monsoon season (April to June); in northern regions the hottest month is May.
s: Grishma
Summer or pre-monsoon; May for the north

questions.q: (a) In winter the average temperature in the north-west is around 10 to 15 degrees Celsius and in the south-east of the mainland around 20 to 25 degrees Celsius. By how much is the south-east warmer at each end of the range? (b) What does this tell you about the effect of the equator on winter temperature?
questions.a: (a) 20 - 10 = 10 degrees and 25 - 15 = 10 degrees, so the south-east is about 10 degrees Celsius warmer. (b) The chapter says temperatures increase towards the equator, so winter is milder in the places nearer to it.
s: About 10 degrees Celsius warmer
Temperatures increase towards the equator, so milder winters in the south

questions.q: Why is the post-monsoon season also called the 'retreating monsoon', and which part of India gets more rain at that time?
questions.a: Monsoon rain begins to recede from north India at the beginning of October, so the monsoon is retreating. South India typically receives more rainfall during this time.
s: Monsoon rain recedes from north India from the beginning of October
South India receives more rainfall then

questions.q: Which early Indian text recorded scientific measurements of rainfall, and for which two public purposes were the records used?
questions.a: Kauṭilya's Arthaśhāstra; the records were applied in managing the country's revenue and relief efforts.
s: Kautilya's Arthashastra
Managing revenue and relief efforts

questions.q: Rohit says, 'In western and southern India the hottest month, April, comes before the rainy season, so the heat peaks before the monsoon arrives.' Is he right? Support your answer from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter says that in western and southern regions the hottest month is April, which lies in the summer or pre-monsoon season (April to June), and that the monsoon season spans June to September, so the heat peak comes before the monsoon.
s: Verdict: Yes
April is the hottest month in the west and south, in the pre-monsoon season
Monsoon season is June to September, later

questions.q: A student writes: 'In traditional India there are four seasons, each about two months long, covering the year.' Show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: Four seasons of about two months make 4 x 2 = 8 months, which does not cover the 12 months of the year. The chapter says the traditional division is into six seasons (spring, summer, monsoon, early autumn, late autumn, winter), each about two months long, which gives 6 x 2 = 12.
s: 4 x 2 = 8 months, not 12
The chapter's six seasons of about two months
6 x 2 = 12 covers the year

questions.q: Write a three-line diary entry of someone living in north-western India in December, using three facts from the chapter, so that a reader can tell the IMD season without being told its name.
questions.a: Any entry using three of: the cold of December, among the coldest months; the average temperature around 10 to 15 degrees Celsius; December is within a season that runs to early April; October and November have just passed (cloudless) and the monsoon has gone. The entry should point to winter (or to the post-monsoon turn into winter).
s: First fact from the chapter, correctly used
Second fact, correctly used
Third fact; the season can be identified

questions.q: Compare the IMD's four seasons with the traditional six seasons on the basis of the division, the number of seasons, the length of each season and the names, and explain why a Himalayan student may use more than four.
questions.a: IMD seasons: winter, summer or pre-monsoon, monsoon or rainy, post-monsoon or retreating, four in number, of unequal length (for example monsoon June to September, winter December to early April). Traditional seasons: six, each about two months long, based on the astronomical division of the 12 months into six parts, and named Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemanta and Shishira. A Himalayan student may use more than four because the more temperate Himalayan states have two additional seasons, autumn and spring.
s: IMD: four seasons named
IMD lengths unequal, with an example
Traditional: six seasons of about two months, from dividing 12 months by six
Traditional names or their months
Himalayan states add autumn and spring

questions.q: A student uses the chapter's temperature ranges: winter in the north-west is around 10 to 15 degrees Celsius and summer across most of inland India is 32 to 40 degrees Celsius. (i) Find the middle value of each range. (ii) Find the difference between the two middle values. (iii) Explain why the chapter gives a range and not one number. (iv) Name the two coldest months for the north-west.
questions.a: (i) Winter (10 + 15) / 2 = 12.5 degrees Celsius; summer (32 + 40) / 2 = 36 degrees Celsius. (ii) 36 - 12.5 = 23.5 degrees Celsius. (iii) The temperature differs from place to place across the region and from month to month within a season, so a range is truer than a single number. (iv) December and January.
s: Winter middle value 12.5
Summer middle value 36
Difference 23.5
A range, because places and months within a season differ
December and January

questions.q:
A school diary committee wants a one-page guide to the seasons. Version 1 uses the four IMD seasons. Version 2 uses the six traditional Ṛtus. The committee counts whole months: winter December to March (4 months), summer April to June (3 months), monsoon June to September (4 months) and post-monsoon October to December (3 months).
(a) Add the months of the four IMD seasons.
(b) Why is the total more than the 12 months of a year, and which two months are counted twice?
(c) What do the six Ṛtus add up to, and what does this show about them?
(d) The guide can carry only one version. Decide which one, and justify your choice, saying what the other version would have done better.
questions.a: (a) 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 months. (b) Seasons overlap at their edges: December falls in both winter and post-monsoon, and June in both summer and monsoon, so 14 - 12 = 2 months are counted twice. (c) 6 x 2 = 12 months, with no overlap: the Ṛtus divide the year evenly. (d) Either choice is defensible: IMD seasons match the weather department's seasons and show the monsoon plainly but overlap; the Ṛtus fit the Indian calendar months in equal blocks. Credit a choice that uses (a) to (c) and names what the other would have done better.
s: 14 months
Overlap: December and June counted twice
12 months, equal blocks with no overlap
Reasoned choice naming what the other version does better

questions.q:
Harpreet lives in north-western India and Selvam in the south-east of the mainland. The cousins want to hold an outdoor family function in the post-monsoon season, October to December, and can choose only one of the two homes. The chapter says that in the post-monsoon season October and November are usually cloudless in the north-west, that monsoon rain begins to recede from north India at the beginning of October and that South India typically receives more rainfall during this time. It also says that winter temperatures are around 10 to 15 degrees Celsius in the north-west and 20 to 25 degrees Celsius in the south-east.
(a) Which IMD season is October to December?
(b) Which cousin's region is likely to see more rain in this period?
(c) By how much do the winter temperatures of the two regions differ at the lower end of the range?
(d) Decide which home should host the function, and justify your choice using both rain and temperature.
questions.a: (a) Post-monsoon, also called the retreating monsoon. (b) Selvam's (South India receives more rainfall as the monsoon retreats). (c) 20 - 10 = 10 degrees Celsius. (d) Either choice is defensible: Harpreet's home is cloudless in October and November but the winter cold of 10 to 15 degrees begins in December; Selvam's home is warmer, 20 to 25 degrees, but wetter in this period. Credit a decision that weighs both rain and temperature and names what the other home offers.
s: Post-monsoon (retreating monsoon)
South-east, Selvam's region
10 degrees Celsius
Reasoned decision using rain and temperature, naming what the other offers

questions.q: In December, most of India is dry, yet coastal districts of Tamil Nadu receive rain. A student asks why. Which answer is supported by the chapter?
questions.a: The winter or north-east monsoon winds blow from land to sea and are cold and dry, but over the Bay of Bengal they pick up moisture and bring rain to the eastern coast, especially Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and parts of Karnataka.
o: Cold, dry north-east winds pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and rain on the eastern coast
Warm, moist south-west winds blow from the ocean to the land and drench the eastern coast in winter
Winds blowing from land to sea carry their own moisture from the Himalayas to the eastern coast
The landmass heats faster than the ocean in winter, so moist winds rush over the eastern coast

questions.q: In a classroom model, a tray of sand (for land) and a tray of water (for ocean) are heated equally under a lamp, and the sand becomes much warmer. Which statement carries the model over to the south-west monsoon correctly?
questions.a: In summer the Indian landmass heats faster than the surrounding oceans, which creates a low-pressure area over the subcontinent while the ocean stays cooler with high pressure. Winds move from high to low pressure, so moist winds blow from ocean to land.
o: Air over the warm sand rises, giving low pressure there, so air moves in from over the cooler water
Air over the warm sand sinks, giving high pressure there, so air moves out towards the cooler water
Air over the cool water rises, giving low pressure there, so air moves in from over the warm sand
Air over both trays stays still, because land and ocean heat at the same rate in summer

questions.q: A district gets far too much south-west monsoon rainfall one year and far too little the next. Which pair of consequences does the chapter attach to these two years?
questions.a: The chapter says excessive rainfall can cause floods, while weak monsoons can lead to droughts. It also says a good monsoon ensures sufficient food and water supply, which is not the case in either of these two years.
o: Floods in the first year and drought in the second
Drought in the first year and floods in the second
Floods in both years, since monsoon rain always floods
Good harvests in both years, since rain helps crops

questions.q: Arab traders on sailing ships noticed that on the same sea route the winds blew in opposite directions at different times of year, and gave the pattern a name from their own language. Which statement matches the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the Arabs named the seasonal reversal of the wind system 'monsoon', derived from the Arabic mausim, which literally means season. Aurora is a Latin word from the same chapter about the polar lights.
o: They named the seasonal wind reversal 'monsoon', from the Arabic mausim, meaning season
They named the steady trade wind 'monsoon', from the Arabic word mausim, meaning rain
They named the seasonal wind reversal 'monsoon', from the Latin word aurora, meaning dawn
They named the sea route itself 'monsoon', from the Arabic mausim, meaning sailing ship

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the monsoon.
1. During the summer the landmass of India heats up faster than the surrounding oceans.
2. Varāhamihira in his Bṛihatsaṁhitā based rainfall prediction mainly on the positions of the Moon and the Sun.
3. In the south-west monsoon season India has high pressure over land and low pressure over the ocean.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false: the Moon-and-Sun technique is that of Kṛiṣhiparāśhara, while Varāhamihira used the lunar mansions (nakṣhatras). Statement 3 is false: it is low pressure over the land and high pressure over the ocean. Correct: 1 only.
o: 1 only
1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The south-west monsoon winds bring rain to India.
Reason (R): The word monsoon refers to the seasonal reversal in the wind direction during a year.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true: the chapter defines monsoon as the seasonal reversal in wind direction and says south-west monsoon winds bring rain. But the reversal in direction is not why they bring rain; the rain arrives because the moist winds blow from the ocean to a low-pressure land.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: The Moon takes about 27 days to go round the sky and crosses one nakṣhatra a day, so in 54 days it completes ___ full rounds.

Match each name in Column I with what the chapter says about it in Column II.
1. Kṛiṣhiparāśhara
2. Bṛihatsaṁhitā
3. Meghadūtam
4. Mission Mausam
a. Predicts rainfall using lunar mansions (nakṣhatras)
b. Rainfall method based on the positions of the Moon and the Sun
c. Mentions the date of the onset of the monsoon over central India
d. Aims to make India 'Weather Ready' and 'Climate Smart'
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: Kṛiṣhiparāśhara used the positions of the Moon and the Sun; Varāhamihira's Bṛihatsaṁhitā used the lunar mansions; Kālidāsa's Meghadūtam mentions the date of onset over central India; Mission Mausam aims to make the nation Weather Ready and Climate Smart.

questions.q: True or False: Because the north-east monsoon winds blow from land to sea, they bring no rainfall anywhere in India. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: False. These cold, dry winds generally do not bring rain to most parts of India, but after crossing the Bay of Bengal they pick up moisture and cause rain on the eastern coast, especially in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and parts of Karnataka.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: they pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and rain falls on the eastern coast

questions.q: (a) In which season and in which months does the Indian landmass heat up faster than the surrounding oceans? (b) What pressure does this create over the land, and which way do the winds then blow?
questions.a: (a) In the summer, the south-west monsoon months of June to September. (b) A low-pressure area forms over the Indian subcontinent, while the cooler ocean has high pressure; winds blow from the ocean towards the land, bringing rainfall.
s: Summer, June to September
Low pressure over land; winds from ocean to land

questions.q: (a) The Moon moves through one nakṣhatra each day. How many nakṣhatras does it cross in 10 days? (b) The Moon takes about 27 days to go round the sky. After 60 days, how many full rounds has it made and how many extra days remain?
questions.a: (a) 10 nakṣhatras. (b) 60 = 2 x 27 + 6, so 2 full rounds and 6 extra days.
s: 10 nakshatras
2 full rounds and 6 days

questions.q: Give two ways, other than farming, in which the monsoon touches the daily life of people in India, according to the chapter.
questions.a: Any two of: daily life, transport, festivals, employment (especially in rural areas); the supply of water in rivers, reservoirs and wells.
s: First valid effect
Second valid effect

questions.q: Why were sailors who travelled in ancient times among the first to notice the monsoon, and how did they benefit from it?
questions.a: They travelled by sailing ships at the mercy of the winds, so they noticed that the winds reversed with the season; they benefited from this reversal of the wind system in their voyages.
s: They sailed at the mercy of the winds and noticed the reversal
They benefited from the seasonal reversal for their journeys

questions.q: State the two aims by which Mission Mausam describes the nation, and name two sectors that the mission's improved services are meant to help.
questions.a: It aims to make the nation 'Weather Ready' and 'Climate Smart'. Sectors include agriculture, disaster management and rural development (any two).
s: Weather Ready and Climate Smart
Any two sectors from agriculture, disaster management, rural development

questions.q: Dhruv says, 'The south-west monsoon brings all of India's rain, so the winter monsoon hardly matters anywhere.' How far is he right? Use the chapter.

questions.q:
A village council in a farming region keeps two almanacs. One follows Kṛiṣhiparāśhara and the other follows Varāhamihira's Bṛihatsaṁhitā. The council can print only one in the new village hall, or choose the forecasts of the National Monsoon Mission models instead. On 1 June the Moon was in nakṣhatra number 5 and moves through one nakṣhatra each day; there are 27 nakṣhatras and after number 27 it returns to number 1.
(a) Which technique does each almanac use?
(b) In which nakṣhatra will the Moon be on 20 June, and on 30 June?
(c) Why did Indians work out such methods?
(d) Decide which one the council should print, and justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) Kṛiṣhiparāśhara: positions of the Moon and the Sun; Bṛihatsaṁhitā: lunar mansions (nakṣhatras). (b) 20 June is 19 days later: 5 + 19 = 24, so nakṣhatra 24; 30 June is 29 days later: 5 + 29 = 34, which is 34 - 27 = 7, so nakṣhatra 7. (c) Crop production often depended on seasonal monsoon rains, so they worked out methods to predict rainfall. (d) Either choice is defensible: the traditional almanac is a heritage that many farming practices still follow, while the National Monsoon Mission models are state-of-the-art and meant to improve predictions over all time frames. Credit a choice that names what is lost.
s: Moon and Sun positions; lunar mansions
Nakshatra 24 on 20 June and 7 on 30 June
Crop production depended on the monsoon rains
Reasoned choice naming what the other offers
